newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mortgage rates fall in week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mortgage rates fall in week.

text.p: U.S. mortgage rates edged lower this week as interest rates fell after comments by Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan eased concerns about inflation, Freddie Mac said Thursday.
Thirty-year mortgage rates fell in the week ending July 25 to an average of 7.43 percent from 7.47 percent last week. Fifteen-year mortgage rates slid to 6.98 percent from 7.01 percent.
One-year adjustable mortgage rates fell to 5.54 percent from 5.55 last week.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 8.19 percent, the 15-year 7.71 percent and the adjustable loan 6.01 percent.
Greenspan said in testimony to House and Senate committees this week that U.S. economic growth appears to be slowing, heading off inflation concerns.

"Chairman Greenspan's remarks earlier in the week greatly reassured the financial markets that inflation is not a threat and the economy is in very good condition," Freddie Mac chief economist Robert Van Order said in a statement.
"Not only did this news help to lower interest rates slightly this week, but it may have the same effect on rates next week."
Fees and points charged by lenders for 30-year and 15-year loans slipped to an average of 1.7 percent from 1.8 percent last week. Adjustable loan charges were unchanged at 1.4 percent.
Freddie Mac is a corporation chartered by Congress that buys mortgages from lenders and packages them into securities for investors.
